source.title: Investigating Why Contrastive Learning Benefits Robustness Against Label Noise
source.authors: Yihao Xue; Kyle Whitecross; Baharan Mirzasoleiman

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices. Some results are presented only in figures.
record.tranche_reason: Reports experiments on deep networks pretrained with contrastive learning and fine-tuned on noisy labels, a distinct training setting for label-noise robustness. It does not reproduce the original random-label experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper cites the claim that first-order gradient methods can fit random labels, but that cited result is not this study's result. Its own experiments use randomly flipped or real-world noisy labels, not completely random labels. Table 1 reports test accuracy under noisy labels but not training error on the noisy labels, so those accuracies do not establish the perfect-fitting behavior in V1 or V4.
record.test_reason: The study's own early-training results bear on V6: contrastively pretrained networks achieve high test accuracy before overfitting noisy labels. Figure 2(c–d) and Sections 4.2–4.3 describe a separation between learning clean signal and memorizing noise. The record overlooks the clean-learning evidence accompanying its noisy-example loss rows.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. More precisely, the authors prove robustness for a linear head on contrastive representations under stated structural assumptions, attribute delayed early noise overfitting during full-network fine-tuning to the initial Jacobian spectrum, and show improved performance when pretraining is combined with robust training methods. Full-network fine-tuning can eventually overfit.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SimCLR pretraining followed by fine-tuning or linear-head training on noisy labels; does not apply the original random-label intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported early overfitting comparison uses CIFAR-10 with 80% randomly flipped labels and contrasts a randomly initialized network with a SimCLR-pretrained network. The paper also reports that fine-tuning all layers eventually overfits if training continues longer.

fits_no_version.finding: Contrastive pretraining delays the reduction of loss on mislabeled examples relative to random initialization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Contrastive pretraining changes the timing of noise memorization. This initialization comparison alone does not establish V2's random-versus-true-label training-time claim.

record.problems: The early-training loss comparison is figure-only and gives no numeric values or uncertainty. It uses one dataset, noise level, and comparison between initialization settings. The experiment does not measure training error on the corrupted labels across noise fractions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows. Table 1 reports test accuracies for methods and noise conditions, but those results do not measure fitting of random labels or training error on corrupted labels.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged training hyperparameters.
Time to fit random versus true labels and convergence time across corruption fractions. Comparing initializations at one noise level does not test these.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect fitting of corrupted training labels throughout a corruption sweep and degradation through complete randomization. Reported training accuracy is evaluated against clean ground-truth labels.
The stated weight-decay, dropout, and augmentation interventions and generalization after their removal.

Completely random labels and the generality of the learning order beyond the tested noisy-label setting; the relative timing for the randomly initialized control is not established by the supplied textual description.

missing.what: The paired test-accuracy trajectories in Figure 2(c), especially the pretrained network's high early accuracy before noisy-label overfitting. Record these alongside R1–R2 so the evidence for learning clean signal before noise is visible. Exact curve values are unavailable in the supplied text.

record.verdict_notes: No evidence establishes zero training error on corrupted labels. The frozen linear-head guarantees concern a different system from the standard trainable deep networks named in V1–V5 and do not challenge those versions.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labels, zero or near-zero training error, chance test error, and keeping architecture and training hyperparameters unchanged.
Training-time comparison for random versus true labels and convergence versus corruption fraction.
Fitting shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
The study varies the fraction of randomly flipped labels and reports test accuracy, but does not report whether training error on the corrupted labels remains perfect across those fractions.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent fitting random labels, or whether removing them harms generalization on true labels.
The study reports loss on mislabeled examples over training, but does not compare learning of shared real-label patterns with learning of noisy labels to establish their order or difference.
